title: Count multiples of any divisor
prompt: Write countDivisibleByAny(n int64, divisors []int64) int64 returning how many integers in [1, n] are divisible by at least one entry of divisors. The divisors are distinct and at least 2 but need not be coprime, n goes up to 10^18, and there can be up to 30 divisors, so neither walking the range nor visiting all 2^30 subsets fits in the time limit.
explanation: The count of integers up to n divisible by d is exactly n/d with integer division, so the only difficulty is that the sets overlap. Inclusion-exclusion fixes that: add the singletons, subtract the pairs, add the triples, and so on, where a subset's shared multiples are the multiples of the subset's lcm, not its product. Using the product is the classic wrong answer and it is wrong the moment two divisors share a factor: {4, 6} overlap on multiples of 12, not of 24. Two implementation points carry the drill. First, the recursion must prune. Written as a mask loop over 2^30 subsets it is a billion iterations regardless of how cheap the body is, but written as a depth-first walk that carries the running lcm, a node whose lcm already exceeds n can be abandoned with its whole subtree, because n/lcm is zero there and stays zero under every further lcm. With 30 small primes and n around 2*10^8 that leaves only the few thousand subsets whose product actually fits under n. Second, the lcm must never be formed when it would not fit: a/gcd(a,b)*b overflows int64 for subsets of large divisors, so compare a/gcd(a,b) against n/b first and report 'past n' instead of multiplying. On this input the overflow happens to be harmless (a wrapped value is huge in magnitude, so n divided by it truncates to zero), but that is luck, not a guarantee, and the divide-first check costs nothing.
hints: Two divisors that share a factor overlap on multiples of what number, and how is that different from their product?
If the running value for a partial subset is already bigger than n, what does every superset of it contribute?
Before forming a*b, what comparison tells you the result would be past n without doing the multiply?

title: Expected turns with a wasted move
prompt: A token starts at 0 and you want it on n. Each turn you draw a step k with probability p[k] for k in 0..len(p)-1; the token advances to i+k, except that a step that would carry it past n is wasted and it stays on i. Write expectedSteps(n int, p []float64) float64 returning the expected number of turns to land exactly on n. The p entries sum to 1 and p[1] is strictly positive. n goes up to 200000 and len(p) up to 200.
explanation: Write E[i] for the expected turns remaining from position i, with E[n] = 0. One turn always costs 1, then you land somewhere: E[i] = 1 + sum over k of p[k] * E[destination]. The catch is that some of those destinations are i itself, so E[i] appears on both sides and the equation is not a recurrence yet. Collect that mass into a single stay probability s(i) = p[0] plus every p[k] with i+k > n, and the equation becomes E[i] = 1 + s(i)*E[i] + sum over the reachable k of p[k]*E[i+k], which rearranges to E[i] = (1 + sum) / (1 - s(i)). That division is the whole drill. Note s(i) is position dependent, not a constant: near the end of the board more steps overshoot, so more mass loops back. Dividing by 1 - p[0] alone is right in the middle of the board and wrong in the last len(p) positions. The other tempting mistake is to treat an overshoot as arriving, which turns a wasted turn into a win and undercounts. With the self loop eliminated, E depends only on strictly larger indices, so one backward pass in O(n * len(p)) finishes it, and p[1] > 0 guarantees 1 - s(i) is at least p[1] so the division is always safe. Value iteration, repeatedly applying the one-step update until it settles, gets the same numbers and is what the tests use as an independent check, but it converges at a rate set by the stay probability and is far too slow when that probability is near 1.
hints: Which of the outcomes of one turn leave the token exactly where it started, and what does that do to the equation for E[i]?
Is the probability of standing still the same at position 0 as at position n-1?
Once E[i] no longer appears on its own right-hand side, which direction does the sweep go?

title: Count every pattern in one pass
prompt: Write countOccurrences(text string, patterns []string) []int returning, for each pattern in order, how many times it occurs in text, counting overlapping occurrences. Everything is lowercase a-z, patterns may repeat, and the tests run 150000 patterns against a 2000000 character text, so searching for one pattern at a time is out even with a fast substring search.
explanation: Aho-Corasick is KMP with a trie in place of the single pattern. Put all patterns in a trie, then give every node a fail link pointing at the node for the longest proper suffix of that node's string which is also a node in the trie, exactly the KMP failure function generalised. Build the links breadth-first so that when you process a node its parent's link is already final. The step that makes the scan O(1) per character is turning the trie into a full automaton: for a character with no real child, overwrite that slot with wherever the fail link's automaton would send it. Because the fail link is shallower and therefore already finished, this is one array read, and after it the scan is a single state variable and one lookup per character with no while loop and no worst case blowup. Counting is where a naive implementation goes quadratic: at each text position the matches ending there are the current node plus everything reachable by following fail links, and walking that chain can cost O(pattern length) per character. Instead just increment a counter on the node you land on, and after the scan push those counters down the fail tree in reverse BFS order, so each node accumulates the hits of every node that fails into it. That is one linear pass over the nodes for all patterns at once. Repeated patterns need no special handling because they land on the same terminal node. Total cost is O(total pattern length * alphabet + text length + node count), against O(patterns * text) for searching one at a time, which is the difference between a fifth of a second and a minute and a half on these inputs.
hints: What is the KMP failure function for a set of patterns rather than one, and what does a node's link have to point at?
If you rewrite the missing child slots instead of leaving them empty, how many lookups does one text character cost?
Following the chain of links at every text position is quadratic. Can the totals be pushed along that chain once at the end instead?
refs: Aho and Corasick 1975, Efficient string matching
